I write a program that compiles and appears to work and has been checked over by other programmers for months. Someone posts a tweet on X saying that ChatGPT found errors in the program, with nary a hint as to what those errors are.

That's nuts, right? If a compiler -- a kind of proof engine -- finds errors, there are errors. Fix them! Don't complain about the usage of a compiler, the errors were real, they're there, they need to be fixed.

The fuzziness part is both useful and a liability, but the error rate is dropping.

Some numbers for you:

A year ago, I ran a huge legacy codebase through Gemini Pro 2.5 and it spat out several thousand bugs, but manual inspection showed that 80% were false positives and only 20% were worth fixing.

I did a similar exercise with GPT 5.6 more recently, and the hit rate was 80% valid and 20% false positive. The human developer got into an argument saying that they thought all 100% were false positives. He lost. The AI could easily produce "repro" snippets that triggered every issue (mostly security vulnerabilities, but some correctness ones too).

These days, if you're publishing anything with verifiable claims in it, and not running it through an AI first, it's the direct equivalent of uploading open source code to GitHub without bothering to check that it compiles first.

It's sloppy.
I'm not arguing that LLMs aren't useful tools for mathematicians, I'm questioning the quality of discourse that amounts to "I pasted this into the LLM and it said there are errors".

An interesting thing about the Riemann hypothesis is that there are a lot of other conjectures that have no obvious connection to it but that turn out to be equivalent. Equivalent in this context means that if any of them are true then all of them are.

Here is one that is easy to understand with a high school level of math:

Let H(n) = 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ... + 1/n, where n is a positive integer.

Let D(n) = the sum of the positive integers that divide a positive integer n. For example D(12) = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 6 + 12 = 28.

Conjecture: For n > 1, we have D(n) < H(n) + exp(H(n)) log(H(n)).

With so many different conjectures turning out to be equivalent, I'll not be surprised if it turns out that there are also multiple different ways to prove it.

Not necessarily. There isn't any specific amount price has to move as a result of a change in supply.

On my reread, it sounded to me like John Henry's boss was bringing in steam drills to work. And John Henry read it as a threat or invalidation of his value.

What I was trying to say is that John Henry was much more valuable than his ability to drive steel. If he was able to get really good at something hard or valuable enough to be respected for it, he was probably just strong and hardworking and conscientious enough to succeed in any similarly physical task.

To be blunt, jobs only exist as long as there is demand for the labor and whatever thing the labor enables the employer to profit from. They go away and move around not because employers make decisions to screw workers, but because the job's existence is contingent on it being something someone wants to pay for, because it helps them somehow.

John Henry could have found a new job if he had the self confidence to believe he was more valuable than in his ability to fill a role that was only ever going to exist in a particular place and time.

The point of the John Henry story isn't that machines are replacing humans, just like the argument against manufacturing (etc) automation isn't that humans are being automated out of their jobs.
